transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Alex Turner (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Pegasus SRE), Marta Alvarez (Pegasus CSM), Liam Chen (Pegasus Head of Platform)

Summary:
Quick postmortem follow-up after last week's outage that impacted Pegasus Health inference endpoints (approx 90 minutes of degraded responses). Focus: confirm root cause, discuss mitigations already applied, runbook changes, dedicated vs hosted options, and plan for benchmarks/validation.

Topics:
- Incident recap and timeline
- Root cause: KV cache eviction + autoscaler bug + burst traffic pattern
- Short-term mitigations deployed (fallback routing, temporary throttling)
- Long-term reliability work: autoscaler fix, warmed-up KV caches, dedicated pool recommendation
- Roadmap: benchmarks, runbook changes, SLA additions

Action items and next steps were captured (see metadata).

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: All right, hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda - walk through the postmortem, what we rolled out yesterday, and then map next steps. Marta, you want to kick us off with what you saw from Pegasus side?
[00:22] Marta: Yeah thanks Alex. So on our side we saw a sudden increase in tail latency starting 10:12 UTC last Tuesday. It lasted about an hour, then flares again later in the day. Users reported slow replies and timeouts. We opened the escalation and worked with Redwood support.
[00:40] Jordan: I can add - from SRE traces we had 503s plus very high server-side queueing, looked like the KV cache (prefix cache) wasn't being hit as expected; we saw cache miss rate jump from ~4% to >70% during the spike.
[00:58] Priya: Right, our initial correlates showed concurrent small-batch traffic pattern and a bug in the autoscaler where it interpreted many short-lived connections as low utilization; it failed to scale fast enough so cold workers were serving, and cold starts + cache misses amplified latency.
[01:18] Liam: And you think it's an interaction between request pattern and the autoscaler heuristics, not, say, a model issue or quantization regression?
[01:27] Priya: Correct, we validated the model binary and weights - no regressions. Quantization profile same as before. This was more about runtime state: KV cache warming and scheduling.
[01:37] Jordan: We also noticed that during the spike some requests were routed to lower-tier nodes due to fallback policy when primary pool hit a soft limit. Those fallback nodes had different CPU affinity and less warmed KV caches.
[01:50] Alex: Ok so we have three contributing factors - bursty traffic pattern increasing miss rates, autoscaler under-reacting, and fallback routing landing on colder nodes. Does that align?
[02:05] Marta: Yeah that's fair. Also worth noting Pegasus had a config change on their side to increase request concurrency from an internal deploy that morning, which changed the shape of traffic.
[02:18] Priya: We rolled out several mitigations: 1) temporarily disabled fallback routing for the affected route to force requests to the dedicated pool; 2) increased autoscaler aggressiveness threshold; 3) seeded KV caches by prewarming with synthetic prefixes. That reduced P95 from ~1.2s to ~380ms in our staged tests.
[02:39] Jordan: We saw improvements after the prewarm. Production numbers look better but we want independent validation, which is why we asked for the benchmark.
[02:50] Alex: Right, the benchmark is next step. Priya, can you describe the plan and the profile you'll run?
[02:55] Priya: Sure. We'll run a 10k-request sweep using Pegasus request shapes - mix of 64/256/512 token requests, 60/120/200 rps sweeps, both hosted and a temporary dedicated pool with same instance type. We'll capture P50/P95/P99, cold-start fraction, cache hit/miss metrics, and token cost per request. We'll also run with and without the prewarm routine and with slightly different autoscaler thresholds.
[03:22] Liam: For acceptance, we want P95 < 450ms for 512-token requests at 200 rps. If Redwood can show that on dedicated pool with prewarm + autoscaler fix, Pegasus prefers dedicated.
[03:37] Alex: Noted. One common question we see: why didn't fallback detection trigger earlier? Priya?
[03:45] Priya: The heuristics are conservative to avoid flapping; in this case the metric used by autoscaler (average utilization over X seconds) smoothed the spike and didn't scale quickly. We'll propose a change to consider short-window percentiles - e.g., 95th-utilization over 20s windows - as a complementary signal.
[04:04] Jordan: Will that increase unnecessary scale-ups in noisy workloads? We have spiky telemetry normally.
[04:12] Priya: Good point - we'll implement it as an additional signal with a cooldown and cap, and tie it to route-level config so Pegasus can tune it only for routes with known bursty patterns.
[04:22] Marta: On the security/compliance side, we had a question earlier about logs retention during the incident - did Redwood store unredacted traces anywhere?
[04:31] Alex: We keep request/response traces in a secured bucket for 30 days for incidents; access is RBAC-controlled. For Pegasus we can provide redacted traces and the subset you need. We also have KMS integration for encryption at rest.
[04:43] Liam: SOC 2 and ISO - are the incident artifacts part of the audit? Pegasus needs the chain of custody.
[04:50] Alex: Yes, we can produce an audit bundle: timeline, console logs, who accessed artifacts. We'll coordinate with Security for the formal bundle, link to the SOC 2 report, and include audit log exports.
[05:02] Jordan: We'd like the raw traces for our SRE to correlate with our own telemetry. We'll redact PII but keep timing and request ids.
[05:11] Marta: Also, on the process side, we want to update the runbook to include: prewarm script for high-burst campaigns, a manual override to pin traffic to dedicated pool, and alerting for KV cache miss rate > 20% for 2 minutes.
[05:28] Priya: Agreed - Redwood can add runbook templates and a playbook for toggling fallback routing and initiating prewarm. We'll also expose the autoscaler config as a route-level knob in the console so you can tune on the fly.
[05:44] Alex: Pricing question the team raised - moving to dedicated will increase monthly committed spend. Jordan, Marta - what's the threshold for Pegasus to accept that tradeoff?
[05:53] Marta: From product, we care about uptime and predictability during campaigns. If dedicated reduces incidents and keeps latency predictable, the execs are fine with a higher commit, as long as we can measure unit cost and show improvements.
[06:05] Liam: We also want an option for mixed model: keep base on hosted and burst into dedicated during high-volume campaigns; need warm-up strategy for burst capacity.
[06:15] Priya: That's exactly one of the capabilities we support - dynamic routing with burst capacity. The key is making sure the dedicated pool is warmed and the prewarm runs before routing changes.
[06:27] Jordan: For the benchmark, please include a scenario where 30% of traffic is suddenly shifted from hosted to dedicated to simulate a campaign spike.
[06:36] Priya: Will do. We'll also capture cold-start percent across the mix.
[06:42] Alex: Any outstanding compliance blockers for running the benchmark?
[06:45] Marta: We only need to ensure test payloads are PII-free; we can provide synthetic data. Also need confirmation that temporary dedicated pool won't store customer keys locally - KMS still used?
[06:56] Priya: KMS is used in both hosted and dedicated; keys never leave your KMS if you bring-your-own. We'll document the flow.
[07:04] Jordan: On longer-term mitigations, are there changes to scheduling, kernel selection, or model variants we should consider?
[07:12] Priya: Potentially. For certain prompts with long prefix locality we can optimize KV cache layout and evict less aggressively. Also, we can recommend specific quantization settings that preserve throughput while reducing memory pressure. But these are model-specific and we'll pair with your ML team.
[07:28] Marta: Good. Can we also get a short list of console alerts/log queries we should add?
[07:34] Priya: Yes - we'll provide a four-item list: KV cache miss rate, worker cold-start count, route fallback rate, and end-to-end P95 for the route.
[07:45] Alex: Ok, wrapping up - quick recap and owners?
[07:49] Marta: (interrupting) also want to confirm the SLA conversation - given this incident, can we get a better latency SLA for the route?
[07:56] Alex: We'll have Redwood legal and your procurement talk SLA addendum - typical path is commit to dedicated capacity plus SLA. We'll start that conversation; Alex will loop legal.
[08:06] Liam: timeline?
[08:08] Alex: We'll send the initial postmortem deck tomorrow (11/29). Benchmarks will run early next week, results by 12/03. Runbook session week of 12/06. Legal/procurement thread to start once Pegasus confirms target commit.
[08:22] Jordan: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[08:25] Priya: Thanks - I'll follow up with the benchmark plan and required payloads.
[08:29] Alex: Great. End time 15:48 UTC.
